item.title: Turtles nested in record numbers at Great Nicobar project site: RTI reply confirms Scroll report
item.description: Turtle nesting sites qualify for the highest levels of coastal protection, contradicting the NGT’s assertions about environmental clearance for the project.
item.content:encoded:
In March, Scroll reported that sea turtles had nested in record numbers on the beaches of Great Nicobar Island’s Galathea Bay during the 2025-’26 nesting season.

Only the previous month, the National Green Tribunal dismissed challenges to the construction of a mega-infrastructure project on the island, asserting that no part of the project site is a CRZ-1A area – a category of coastal land that has maximum protection under law on account of its ecological importance.

Now, official records from the Andaman and Nicobar Islands Forest Department accessed via a Right to Information application have confirmed the Scroll report.

The March report, based on photographs accessed from Galathea Bay and from conversations with locals, had suggested about 1,000 turtle nests in the area over the November to March nesting period.

The data obtained via the RTI application puts the number of nests in Galathea Bay beach at 997, with 889 being of the leatherback turtle. The other 108 are of the Olive Ridley turtle.

item.title: National law school Bengaluru cancels Umar Khalid documentary screening, 2 days after IIIT Hyderabad
item.description: The censor board has flagged that the film, ‘Prisoner No: 626710 is Present’, has not been certified.
item.content:encoded:
A student committee at the National Law School of India University, Bengaluru has cancelled the screening of a documentary about jailed activist Umar Khalid on its campus, The Hindu reported on Sunday.

Khalid has been in judicial custody for six years in connection with the conspiracy case related to the 2020 Delhi riots. The trial in the case is yet to begin.

The Law and Society Committee told The Hindu that it cancelled the event as the Central Board of Film Certification has said that the documentary, Prisoner No: 626710 is Present, has not been certified.

This came two days after the International Institute of Information Technology, Hyderabad, cancelled a screening of the same documentary following an objection from the censor board.

The film certification body had said on social media that public screening of a documentary that had not been certified by it “is a violation” of the 1952 Cinematograph Act “unless a specific exemption has been sought under the act”.

At the Bengaluru law school, the screening was initially scheduled for September 14. However, the organisers postponed it after the Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad objected to the event.

The ABVP is the student wing of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, the parent organisation of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.

item.title: A new book follows the lives of climate refugees from Bangladesh after Cyclone Aila in 2009
item.description: An excerpt from ‘The Undocumented: One Family’s Journey from Bangladesh to India,’ by Nidhi Dugar Kundalia.
item.content:encoded:
Water seems the bane of her life, following Nur from the Sundarbans all the way here. In the monsoons, it collects in crevices between homes, creating a sweet nesting spot for mosquitoes. When neighbours are on good terms, they collect coins and bring DDT to sprinkle in the puddles. Acrid smoke rises from burning rubber and old sandals, lit by women trying to stretch the cooking fire a little further because firewood costs Rs 5 a kilo.

Nur and Kajal spot a knot of children playing tiktik, humming its sing-song chant. The older girls are away at their Quran classes, held in a makeshift hut run by a nearby mosque, their scarves neatly pinned beneath their chins. One of the children reaches out and grabs Nur’s hand, pulling her briefly into their circle.

Thakuma – small, ashen-haired, the slum’s oldest at barely 58, dengue having taken her family – returns with packets of biscuits under her arm. She walks with a totter, her voice like cracked betel nut: jagged, never unkind. When a child is left hungry and alone because their mother is at work, it’s Thakuma who notices first. item.title: Start the week with a film: In winning comedy ‘Best of the Best’, friendship needs delicate footwork
item.description: Lena Khan’s movie, starring Maitreyi Ramakrishnan and Priyanka Kedia, is out on Netflix.
item.content:encoded:
Childhood friends on a journey of self-discovery participate in a dance competition that causes a rift between them – it sounds like a Bollywood film. But it isn’t.

Best of the Best has a tonne of Indian-origin talent, from the director to the writers and the cast, and a soundtrack that includes musical hits from the country of origin. But the Netflix film is also an entirely American production in its look and spirit, which celebrates connections to the mother ship while also affirming strong moorings in the chosen port of call.

Directed by Lena Khan, and written by Prashanth Venkataramanujam and Hasan Minhaj, the comedy is led by Never Have I Ever star Maitreyi Ramakrishnan and Priyanka Kedia. Ramakrishnan is Maya: smart, individualistic and too blunt for her own good. Kedia is Anjali: academically weaker and a validation seeker but popular in a way Maya isn’t.

Both are adept dancers, especially when paired together. When they enrol in the University of California, Los Angeles, and then join a fusion dance group called Agni, they are on equal footing – for a while. item.title: Why Indian zoos are unsafe for staff
item.description: As a recent tragedy in Jaipur showed, the country does not have standardised guidelines to ensure the safety of those who work with dangerous animals.
item.content:encoded:
Kamla Devi never thought that a casual conversation with a colleague would save her life.

On the morning of September 2, Kamla, her sister Sugna Devi and five other women were cutting grass in a tiger’s enclosure at Jaipur’s Nahargarh Biological Park. The zoo is nestled in the Aravallis, and houses an animal rescue centre and several enclosures of mammals, such as bears, panthers and tigers. The sisters had been employed for cleaning and gardening work since the park’s inauguration in 2016.

As they worked that morning, Devi saw a flash of yellow and black from the corner of her eye – the tiger, named Shivaji, had made its way out from its isolation enclosure to the area where the women were working.

Kamla’s mind instantly returned to an incident from around a year ago, where a young staff member who was showing off tricks, demonstrated to Kamla and Sugna how to climb the wire mesh around the animals’ enclosure.

Kamla began to climb the mesh fence, as did the five other women. Midway, clinging on to the mesh, Kamla looked back to see where her sister was. What she saw still haunts her – the tiger had one paw on Sugna’s chest, and had attacked her neck....

item.title: Canada’s overqualified immigrants suffer at work but companies pay the price too
item.description: Managers cannot fix broader systemic causes but can influence what happens once an overqualified immigrant is on the job.
item.content:encoded:
Canada actively recruits highly educated and skilled immigrants through programs, yet many of these immigrants struggle to find work matching their skills and experience.

Nearly one in three immigrants with a post-secondary education report that they are overqualified for their jobs. Statistics Canada data from 2024 and 2025 puts the figure at 33%, compared with 19% among Canadian-born workers.

Much of the discourse around this issue has focused, understandably, on why skilled immigrants end up in jobs below their qualifications. Their foreign credentials, skills and experience are often undervalued, particularly when they come from non-OECD countries, while employers tend to favour candidates with Canadian experience.

These are critical issues, and efforts to address them must continue. But less attention has been paid to why this mismatch is not only a problem for employees, but also for employers, and what employers can do when an overqualified immigrant is already on the job.

We are researchers in social psychology and international business who study migration, immigrant adaptation and economic mobility, as well as how organisations can better recognise and use the strengths of multicultural employees.

When overqualification goes unaddressed

For immigrants, being overqualified can affect well-being, job satisfaction and their sense of progress in their new country.

item.title: Why it is important to teach students what AI cannot do when it comes to writing
item.description: Students should be taught to distinguish AI’s pattern recognition skills from its inability to inhabit human perspectives and authentically express itself.
item.content:encoded:
It’s disconcerting to envision human thought becoming redundant or deemed inferior due to advancements in artificial intelligence. But for all its ills, AI cannot be ignored or wished away. It’s here to stay, and I want my students to understand the stakes of becoming too reliant on this technology.

I can’t blame them for wondering why they should dedicate so much time and effort to honing their writing and critical thinking skills if large language models appear to do a passable job.

Yet this situation has major implications for culture and societies.

It’s easy to envision a future where AI dependency leads to intellectual conformity and the erosion of critical thinking. Researchers are already documenting these effects, which threaten to render the hard work of wrestling with ideas a lost art.

This is why I think it’s critical for educators to confront AI head-on. The key, I believe, is teaching students to distinguish AI’s pattern recognition skills from its inability to daydream, inhabit human perspectives and authentically express itself.

Tell me what you think

item.title: Assam CM lays foundation for Adani power project on land cleared by evicting 1,400 Muslim families
item.description: The company told the environment ministry that the site had no habitations and involved no rehabilitation or resettlement claims.
item.content:encoded:
Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma on Sunday laid the foundation for a thermal power project to be built by Adani Power Limited in the state’s Dhubri district on land where the homes of 1,400 Bengali-origin Muslim families were demolished in July 2025.

The project is located in Charuabakhra, Chirakuta I and II and Santoshpur villages under the Chapar revenue circle.

In July 2025, the Assam government had demolished the homes of more than 1,400 Bengali-origin Muslim families living on nearly 1,157 acres of government land in these villages to make way for a power project. The land was allotted to the state-run Assam Power Distribution Company Limited, which subsequently allotted it to Adani Power Limited for the project.

Nearly 10,000 Bengali-origin Muslims who had lived in the area for at least three decades to four decades were displaced following the demolitions, Scroll had reported.

A resident had said then that many were “erosion-hit people who lost their ancestral homes due to the Brahmaputra”.

On Sunday, the chief minister said that the 3,200 MW thermal power project was Assam’s “biggest-ever power project” and would generate enough electricity to meet the state’s entire power needs.

item.title: Bengaluru’s Hebbal tunnel is a risk to groundwater and could worsen flooding, say experts
item.description: A part of the tunnel road will run close to the Hebbal Lake, one of the city’s few remaining flood buffer zones.
item.content:encoded:
The proposed three-lane, bidirectional tunnel road in north Bengaluru, intended to ease congestion at Hebbal Junction – a major interchange connecting the airport with the rest of the city – has run into rough weather.

At an estimated Rs 1,385 crore, the tunnel will cost about Rs 622 crore per kilometre. The tunnel’s long-term benefits in terms of easing traffic congestion are, however, unclear.

A recent analysis by the Sustainable Transportation Lab of the Indian Institute of Science points out that the tunnel is a “highly localised improvement” that “merely shifts the congestion point”, leaving bottlenecks at its entry and exit. The detailed project report or DPR shows that by 2047, the tunnel will operate at or beyond capacity in all scenarios modelled.

According to urban mobility expert Satya Arikutharam, apart from creating more chaos at these bottlenecks, the tunnel “will also worsen the local traffic, the very problem it intends to solve. Faster arrival rate at these local road intersections due to the new short tunnel capacity means quicker accumulation of traffic, queuing pile-ups and traffic jams,” he says.

Groundwater and flooding concerns

A bigger concern the citizens and environmental experts are raising is about the risks it could pose to groundwater and flooding.

item.title: Toll in Nepal-China flash floods may reach 10,000, says minister
item.description: As of Saturday, the toll had reached 1,411 and 5,875 were missing.
item.content:encoded:
The toll in the flash flood and mudslide in Nepal and China, which occurred on August 26, is expected to reach 10,000, The Indian Express quoted Nepal Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle as saying on Saturday.

The toll had reached 1,411 and 5,875 were missing as of Saturday, said Nepal’s disaster management authority.

Speaking at an event in New Delhi, Wagle said that those dead and missing included pilgrims, tourists, traders and small businessmen.

He also said that Nepal’s energy infrastructure had been severely hit by the floods, reported The Indian Express.

The country’s energy ministry had earlier stated that the floods had impacted 13 hydropower plants, including several under-construction projects, as well as a solar power plant.

The 14-megawatt Devighat hydropower plant, which supplied electricity to India, was also affected, The Indian Express had reported on August 28.

Last week, the Indian government approved Nepal’s request for an early import of electricity to offset the shortfall caused by the disaster. India will export 654 megawatts of electricity for 18 hours a day from September 13 to December 31 under the agreement.

The floods had occurred in the Rasuwa district along Nepal’s northern border with China. The mountainous district is located about 120 km north of Kathmandu. As there was no rainfall in the area, residents did not have a warning about the deluge.

item.title: ‘Dechoma and the Women of Mahe’: This novel maps girlhood between beauty and its absence
item.description: J Devika’s translation of Fathi Salim’s Malayalam novel preserves a densely local world while revealing the universal tensions of girlhood.
item.content:encoded:
For much of Dechoma and the Women of Mahe, young Umaiba is watching women. She gazes at them as they apply surma, worry about how they look, and slip through emotions she cannot yet name. Umaiba is young and waits at the seemingly pearly gates of womanliness, struck by afflictions of comparison, and yet drawn to the all-knowing mirror.

Written by Fathi Salim in Malayalam and translated by J Devika, Dechoma and the Women of Mahe leans on the tender nerve of the transition from girlhood to womanhood, following Umaiba through the years leading up to her first period. It is a novel of womanhood, womanliness, and women. Around Umaiba gathers an expansive cast of ummas, bellummas, brides, healers, widows and neighbours, each inhabiting womanhood in a plethora of singular registers.

Amid this carnival of femininities, Dechoma presents herself as the most apparent antithesis to womanliness – an ageing woman with dusty feet, paan-stained lips and a stubborn refusal to wear slippers, who becomes the one Umaiba returns to time and again, her presence eliciting comfort and joy. item.title: Chhattisgarh: 19 Bengali workers detained on suspicion of being undocumented Bangladeshis released
item.description: The records of four others who had been picked up were being checked, said the police.
item.content:encoded:
Nineteen of the 23 migrant workers from West Bengal’s Murshidabad who had been detained in Bilaspur district of Chhattisgarh earlier this month on suspicion of being undocumented Bangladeshi citizens were released on Friday, reported The Hindu.

The men, who hail from Murshidabad’s Samserganj and Sahabad were detained on September 4 from their residences in Chunchiapara-Ganesh Nagar under Sirgiti police station.

The police had alleged that they were summoned multiple times with their documents, but failed to appear, reported The Hindu.

However, their families claimed that the police detained the men late at night despite them possessing voter cards, Aadhaar cards and PAN cards.

Bilaspur Senior Superintendent of Police Rajnesh Singh said that 19 of them were released following verification of their names in the voter lists, local administration records, family details and permanent residence documents, reported The New Indian Express.

“Further steps regarding the remaining four will depend on the reports we receive,” Singh was quoted as saying by the newspaper.

The police claimed that their names had been struck off voter lists during the special intensive revision exercise in West Bengal.

item.title: Manipur: Protests break out in Kangpokpi after six Kuki men detained
item.description: The agitators alleged that security personnel had detained the men without providing any reason.
item.content:encoded:
Protests broke out in Manipur’s Kangpokpi district on Saturday after six Kuki men were allegedly detained by security forces, reported PTI.

The protesters burned tyres on the roads and threw stones at government vehicles, the news agency quoted unidentified officials as saying on Sunday. They alleged that security personnel had detained the Kuki men without providing any reason.

They also dug portions of National Highway-2, which goes from Imphal to Dimapur, at Motbung to prevent security forces’ vehicles from moving, the officials alleged. Security personnel fired tear gas to force the protesters to disperse.

The protests had started around 10 pm on Saturday. Some of the demonstrators suffered injuries and were hospitalised.

The six Kuki men were subsequently released, after which the protest ended, reported PTI.

The men were natives of Kholen village, located close to the Naga-dominated Chawangkining village.

Unidentified persons had on Tuesday opened fire in the village at around 10.30 pm, reported India Today NE.

The Committee on Tribal Unity had alleged that cadres of the National Socialist Council of Nagaland-Isak-Muivah and Zeliangrong United Front-Kamson were involved in the firing.

item.title: Sunday book pick: A murder is announced in Gabriel García Márquez’s ‘Chronicle of a Death Foretold’
item.description: First published in Spanish in 1981 as ‘Crónica de una muerte anunciada’, it was translated by Gregory Rabassa. Márquez was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1982.
item.content:encoded:
“‘But no matter how much they tossed the story back and forth, no one could explain to me how poor Santiago Nasar ended up being involved in such a mix-up.’ The only thing they knew for sure was that Angela Vicario’s brothers were waiting for him to kill him.”

Gabriel García Márquez was awarded the 1982 Nobel Prize in Literature. The 120-page novel Chronicle of a Death Foretold was translated into English by Gregory Rabassa and published immediately after. As the Nobel Prize citation noted, this new novel too presented “a richly composed world of imagination, reflecting a continent’s life and conflicts.” Readers in English must have been suitably intrigued by the title, for a few decades earlier, Agatha Christie had attempted this trope in her 1950 Miss Marple mystery, A Murder is Announced. However, unlike Christie who had foretold only the time and place of the murder, Márquez foretells the time, place, the victim, and the perpetrators. By all logic, this should’ve been the end of the story, for the murder is inevitable and its knowledge inspires no one to intercept it.

item.description: Of the 38.2 lakh appeals filed against decisions taken during the voter roll revision process, only around 1.2 lakh had been decided by Wednesday.

Currently, the state has 19 tribunals to hear the appeals filed against decisions taken during the special intensive revision of electoral rolls.

The move to increase the number of tribunals would be in line with the demand of petitioners challenging the voter roll revision exercise.

Prasenjit Bose, the chairperson of the special intensive revision committee of the West Bengal Pradesh Congress Committee, had urged the court to increase the number of tribunals to 42, keeping in mind the municipal polls scheduled for December, reported The Hindu.

In its affidavit filed before the Supreme Court on Wednesday, the poll panel said that it is “proposed that the number of appellate tribunals in the state may be considered for increase to correspond with the number of parliamentary constituencies, so as to facilitate expeditious disposal of the pending appeals”.

item.title: Following a Goan photographer across empires and a global war
item.description: Moving between Portuguese Goa, British India, princely Gwalior and wartime Mesopotamia, Victor Pereira navigated several worlds.
item.content:encoded:
In 1918, a photograph taken in Baghdad captured the officers and soldiers of Dunsterforce, a military unit assembled from across the British Empire during the First World War. The force, organised in the aftermath of the Bolshevik Revolution the previous year and Russia’s withdrawal from the war, was an attempt by the Allied Powers to contain the Ottoman advances in West Asia.

The photograph captures a fleeting moment in this global conflict. By the time it was made, the man behind the lens had travelled almost as far as the war itself, whose battlefields extended from Europe, through Russia and West Asia to Africa and the Pacific.

The photographer was Victor Pereira, a Roman Catholic from the Portuguese colony of Goa, who had established photographic studios in Bombay and the princely state of Gwalior. In trade directories and commercial listings he is consistently identified as P Victor.

By the turn of the twentieth century, Bombay had become the primary destination for Goan migrants in search of mobility and employment. Some arrived as students. Others took on a variety of occupations: as clerks, doctors, lawyers, musicians and domestic workers, among others.

Living in Bombay required them to negotiate competing loyalties. Goans maintained strong ties to their homeland even...

item.title: HC directs Uttar Pradesh Police to provide protection to Hindu-Muslim lesbian couple
item.description: The court noted that the petitioners were adults and had the freedom to live together without interference from their families.
item.content:encoded:
The Allahabad High Court has directed the Uttar Pradesh Police to provide protection to a Hindu-Muslim lesbian couple whose families had threatened their live-in relationship, Bar and Bench reported.

In the order dated September 14, Justice Gautam Chowdhary noted that the petitioners were adults and had the freedom to live together peacefully without interference from their families.

The counsel representing the couple had urged the court to provide them immediate police protection, saying that they belonged to different religions, were unmarried and faced a serious threat to their lives from their family members, the legal news outlet reported.

The state government said that same-sex relationships were not socially accepted, arguing that they have a negative effect on the traditional framework of society.

The court, however, said that under the law laid down by the Supreme Court, two consenting adults have a fundamental right to choose to live together in a live-in relationship, the judge was quoted by The Times of India as having noted.

The judge also observed that the absence of marital recognition does not give anyone the right to violate the dignity or threaten the physical safety of adult citizens.

The Mumbai Police on Saturday filed a first information report against a professor at the Indian Institute of Technology-Bombay, a day after a student at the institute died by suicide, The Times of India reported.

The parents of the student, 20-year-old Sahil Wakode, have alleged that he faced caste-based discrimination at the institute.

The police have filed a case against Professor Suryanarayan Doolla and other unidentified persons on charges of abetment to suicide and under provisions of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes Prevention of Atrocities Act.

IIT-Bombay claimed that during an examination on Friday, Wakode was found using a mobile phone and uploading the question paper on artificial intelligence chatbot ChatGPT to seek answers. Doolla was reportedly the invigilator at the time.

The institute, however, claimed that no disciplinary action was taken against Wakode. “The matter was also discussed with the student by the instructor, the faculty advisor and the Head of the Department, who counselled him and assured him that the incident would not adversely affect his academic career,” it said.

item.description: ‘Men tend to show their machismo by constantly riding either next to me, or trying to overtake me,’ a woman biker said.

The biker, Shivani Chauhan, said that she had repeatedly signalled the driver to maintain a safe distance. Despite this, she alleged, the vehicle continued to pursue her before hitting her deliberately.

She was thrown off her bike. The car sped away.

item.title: ‘The act of writing is un-citizenly’: Amit Chaudhuri talks about his new novel, ‘Château Rouge’
item.description: ‘The primary attachment of a writer is to explore a domain of freedom which verges on the irresponsible, the indifferent, the absurd.’
item.content:encoded:
In Amit Chaudhuri’s ninth novel, Château Rouge, an Indian writer arriving in Paris for a fellowship finds himself in a sublet apartment in Château Rouge, a dense, multicultural quarter sometimes called “Little Africa.” It is not the storied Paris of “Proust’s house and Baldwin’s digs,” of monuments and cafes, nor does it resemble the kind of Parisian grime popularised across the literature and myth around the city. Disconcerted, he fusses over the noise and the dirty pavements, and the various faults in the furniture of his apartment. Though part of him craves a familiar Parisian experience, he is daunted by the prospect of living out clichés, and puts off reading his long-held copy of A Moveable Feast, which is a decades-old present from his wife. But she hands him another gift: the suggestion that Hemingway had no “Hemingway’s Paris” to fall back on when he was there, and might as well have been living in a place like Château Rouge.

Emboldened by this realisation, he begins to chart a renewed path through Paris, via everyday sights and sounds he encounters whilst loitering in the neighbourhood. item.title: How AI could influence our understanding of mathematics: A computer scientist-novelist’s reflections
item.description: Perhaps the new age of mathematics will favour a mind that delights in speculation, leaps of the imagination and a deep sense of aesthetics.

On September 8, OpenAI claimed it had solved the Navier-Stokes problem. “The question of whether smooth three-dimensional fluid motion can break down has remained unresolved for roughly 90 years,” Open AI said. It put 10,000 AI agents to work on it and the task took 88 hours. What might this mean for how we “do” mathematics?


It is not really clear how mathematicians chose to become mathematicians. After all, there are no “creative mathematics” courses for the budding mathematician the way there are “creative writing” courses for the budding storyteller or poet. There are no celebrity mathematicians to crush on (let’s ignore Brian Cox). Mathematics books for children have ominous reassurances of just how fun, just how easy, just how natural the subject is; this is in direct contradiction with the student’s own experience. So either the books are lying or the student is a duffer. Frankly, given the circumstances, it is a wonder anyone becomes a mathematician.

item.title: What is fascism in the present? Two recent books attempt to diagnose these conditions
item.description: How can fascism in the present help explain contemporary technological, social and political dynamics? Two recent books attempt to diagnose these conditions.
item.content:encoded:
“A moment of reckoning has arrived for the West,” reads a recent recruitment ad for Palantir, a Silicon Valley firm that increasingly provides data-driven “intelligence” for intelligence, police and military agencies – as well as blue-chip corporations and non-profits. “On the factory floor, in the operating room, across the battlefield,” the ad intones, “we build to dominate.”

How do we make sense of this convergence between advanced technologies and unapologetic violence, between “rational” AI and a primordial view of the world that seems to revert to a language of blood and soil, friends and enemies, “us” and “them”? In op-eds, talk shows, and political analyses, a single word has risen to prominence: fascism.

As a term, “fascism” is highly provocative, but seemingly untimely. It conjures up powerful images of jackbooted throngs of followers repeating chants and salutes, visions of black-lettered and blood-red banners. Yet these images are typically associated with political orders from a century ago in interwar Europe, a dusty relic from a previous age where “evil” was identified and annihilated.

item.title: Snakebite treatment: Promising research on nanobody antivenoms
item.description: A shared set of nanobodies could potentially be combined and adapted for different geographical regions.
item.content:encoded:
Every year, between 80,000 and 140,000 people die from snakebites worldwide. Hundreds of thousands more are left with amputated limbs or permanent disabilities.

India accounts for roughly half of these deaths, with around 58,000 people dying from snakebites each year. Many of the victims are farmers, labourers and children in rural communities, bitten while working in the fields or walking home after dark.

Yet the basic way we treat snakebite has changed little in more than a century. Traditional antivenom is made using horses: they are injected with small doses of snake venom, prompting their immune systems to produce antibodies. Blood is then collected from the horse and processed to make the antivenom.

This type of antivenom has saved countless lives, but it has drawbacks. The antivenom can vary from batch to batch, cause severe allergic reactions and is expensive to produce.

It can also offer limited protection. For example, in India, antivenom is mainly made using venoms from four snake species known as the “big four”: the Indian spectacled cobra, common krait, Russell’s viper, and saw-scaled viper. But these antivenoms do not always work well against venoms from other snake species, or populations of the same snake species, found across the country.

item.title: ‘The Yellow Metaphor’: Jiban Narah’s poetry signifies luminous precarity through the yellow colour
item.description: Anindita Kar’s translation does not simply transpose language but preserves the tonal grain and ecological timbre of Narah’s poetry.
item.content:encoded:
Jiban Narah’s collection of Assamese lyrics, The Yellow Metaphor, has been translated into English by Anindita Kar. His decades-long practice has given him consummate mastery and imaginative control over the lyric form.

The metaphors and symbols in his poetic representation serve as powerful devices to unearth hidden emotional and intellectual connections. Together, they expand across memories, ecology and contemporary politics. His lyrics emerge from a chemistry of folk inheritance, intuitive perception of the elemental forces, and a sharp insight into their workings. We see his intuitive power at its best to evoke sensual nuances out of the classic elements of the earth – river, rain, flora and fauna, paddy fields, sunshine, moonlight.

A distinct articulation

Almost as soon as Anand Mohan Sahay took charge as India’s commissioner in the British colony of Trinidad in 1950, he began receiving Indian-origin visitors seeking repatriation to India. They were either former indentured labourers or their descendants.

“Some of them are persons of moderately independent means and propose to set up some small trade to maintain themselves for the rest of their lives in India,” Sahay wrote in a December 1950 letter to Foreign Secretary Subimal Dutt. He added that, in some cases, younger, well-off people were willing to financially support parents who wished to die in the land of their birth.

After the indentured labour system was abolished in the Caribbean in 1917, some Indians decided to move to India, while the majority remained in the West Indies. By the time India attained independence in 1947, Trinidad and British Guiana (now Guyana) had more than 3 lakh people of Indian origin. In the late 1940s and early 1950s, Indians in the Caribbean loosely organised a “Back to India” movement, appealing to both the British colonial authorities and the Indian government.

The move reflects concern across the AI industry and more broadly about the dangers of new, rapidly improving systems. Recent high-profile incidents such as OpenAI AI agents hacking another company and hijacking a public website have shown current systems can break out of safety confines – and even more capable systems are in development.

Further complicating AI safety is the tension between safety and performance. Companies will be reluctant to limit the performance of their models in the name of safety for fear of losing ground to competitors. US President Donald Trump has also rejected calls for a slowdown, for fear of losing ground to China.

This means any successful effort at “pacing the rate of capabilities advancement so that risk prevention has time to keep up”, as Amodei puts it, will require significant cooperation between rival companies – and nations.

Indian philosophical schools expend enormous effort to understand the nature of language. It is not an exaggeration to say that sound is the starting point of Indian metaphysics, the foundation from which they construct their idea of nature. They begin with the point that the universe originated from sound. The idea in the Chāndogyopaniṣad that even the smallest has the infinite within it is an example of the universe encapsulated within a sound.

Sound, in their view, has inherent power and can produce changes in a material world. The importance of chanting and the use of sounds in mantras are examples of the innate power in sound, not just in words. item.title: Indonesia’s ‘orangutan capital of the world’ is being destroyed
item.description: The Singkil peat swamp is one of three extraordinary peatlands being cleared for agriculture and palm oil.
item.content:encoded:
Deep within Indonesia’s Leuser Ecosystem, one of the most important peat swamp forests left on Earth is being cleared, drained, and burned.

The Singkil peat swamp is the largest of three remaining coastal peat swamp forests on Sumatra’s west coast, alongside Kluet and Tripa. Together, these extraordinary peatlands form what’s been called “the orangutan capital of the world,” supporting some of the highest densities of Sumatran orangutans (Pongo abelii) ever recorded.

But Singkil is being destroyed.

The Rawa Singkil Wildlife Reserve is nationally protected under Indonesian law. Clearing forest and establishing oil palm plantations inside the reserve is illegal. Yet forest is being cleared and burned, peat is being drained, and canals are being dug into the swamp, lowering water tables and transforming ancient forests into land for agriculture and oil palm. Satellite investigations have documented extensive illegal clearing and plantation expansion inside the reserve.

And Indonesia’s fire season has now begun.

For peatlands, fire can be devastating. Once drained, peat dries out and becomes highly flammable. Fires can smolder deep underground for weeks or even months, continuing to burn beneath the surface and releasing enormous amounts of carbon dioxide stored in the peat for thousands of years. item.title: Delhi: Satya Niketan building collapsed due to ‘callous, criminal conduct’, says HC

The boys – all aged between 17 years and 19 years – were natives of Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh. They were enrolled in colleges of Delhi University.

The High Court said that the students had Delhi “with lots of hopes and dreams”, reported Bar and Bench.

The bench added that students were “flocking to Delhi for higher education” and this was not a new phenomenon.

item.title: A new book looks at how music streaming apps made background music a commercially viable genre
item.description: An excerpt from ‘You Have Not Yet Heard Your Favourite Song: How Streaming Changes Music’, by Glenn McDonald.
item.content:encoded:
The idea of music as a background atmosphere is not new. We had Muzak in elevators. We had Music for Airports. Or, really, in the pre-internet days we mostly didn’t have music in elevators because moving music around physically was expensive. We usually rode elevators in relative silence, unless you counted the wheezing of the steam engines lifting us from the dirt floor to the other floor, or the rustling of the elevator operators’ spats and the delicate flutter of powder falling from their wigs. Brian Eno’s ambient music was a conceptual innovation, a foreground statement about backgrounds, deployed far more often as art than as utility.

But the idea of elevator music was more ubiquitous than the music itself, maybe because the claustrophobic implications of “elevator” music are more memorable than “situational” or “behavioural” music. Regardless, as a listener you probably did not own any Muzak. You might have had an Eno album or Lou Reed’s anti-ambient classic Metal Machine Music or some compilations of art noise. item.title: Maratha quota activist Manoj Jarange-Patil ends fast, gives Maharashtra 3 months to consider demands
item.description: He ended the 20-day hunger strike after a Maharashtra government delegation informed him about the steps it had initiated to meet the demands.

Maratha quota activist Manoj Jarange-Patil on Thursday called off his hunger strike, but warned the Maharashtra government that he would launch a protest in Mumbai if his demands for reservations for the community were not considered within three months, PTI reported.

Jarange-Patil had been on an indefinite hunger strike since August 29 to press for the issuance of Kunbi caste certificates to eligible members of the Maratha community to help them avail reservations in government jobs and education.

The Kunbis form a sub-caste within the Maratha community. They are included in the Other Backward Classes.

Jarange-Patil’s announcement on Thursday came after he held talks with a government delegation comprising two ministers, legislators and officials in Beed district. The activist had halted in Beed while on his way to Mumbai.

The delegation informed Jarange-Patil about the step the government had initiated.

This came after Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis said that the state government would not tolerate intimidating tactics and questioned the timing of the agitation during the Ganesh festival.

The programme is among several events planned in Bharatiya Janata Party-ruled states to mark Modi’s birthday on Thursday.

The earthen lamps will be lit at schools designated under the Chief Minister Schools of High Relevance and Innovation scheme, the news outlet reported. item.description: Weapons were recovered from the site.
item.content:encoded:
Two suspected militants were killed in a gunfight with security personnel in Jammu and Kashmir’s Udhampur district on Wednesday, the Indian Army said.

The Army’s White Knight Corps said that Operation Sohan was launched after inputs indicating the presence of militants in the Brattal area.

The security forces detected suspicious movement after a search operation was launched.

The militants opened fire at the security personnel during the search operation, prompting the forces to retaliate that triggered the gunfight in which the two militants were killed, The Indian Express quoted unidentified officers as saying.

They added that arms and ammunition were recovered from the militants. The process of establishing their identities and affiliations to militant groups is underway.

The counter-terrorism operation in “hostile weather, difficult terrain and poor visibility” involved personnel from the White Knight Corps, Jammu and Kashmir Police and the Central Reserve Police Force, the Army said.

It added that the search operation was still in progress and security forces remained deployed to track and counter any remaining threat.

item.title: When Delhi floods, the villages around it bear the brunt
item.description: Raota on the Delhi-Gurugram border reflects an agricultural landscape shaped by the flows of water and labour between the city and the village.
item.content:encoded:
As the monsoon approached the National Capital Region, residents had to negotiate familiar challenges of waterlogged roads, overflowing drains and urban flooding.

Yet beyond Delhi and Gurugram lies another story that rarely makes headlines: the burden of protecting cities from floods is increasingly being shifted onto peri-urban villages that are at the margins of urban development.

Raota, a village located along the Najafgarh drain on the Delhi-Gurugram border, illustrates this reality. Like many villages on the expanding edges of Indian cities, Raota is neither fully rural nor fully urban.

As per official records, it is one of the remaining 49 rural villages of Delhi. Yet it has no elected village panchayat. In January 1990, the Lieutenant Governor of Delhi issued orders terminating the tenure of village pradhans across Delhi.

Even after the 73rd Constitutional Amendment strengthened Panchayati Raj institutions nationwide, Delhi’s villages were not provided with comparable mechanisms of decentralised local governance.

Such villages are now critical to the functioning of cities. They provide land, water and ecological services that sustain urban growth. At the same time, they absorb the environmental costs of that growth.

item.title: A journalist exposing rape claims against Dera chief was killed. His son awaits justice 24 years on
item.description: The Supreme Court will soon hear a plea against the overturning of Gurmeet Ram Rahim Singh’s conviction in the 2002 murder of Ram Chander Chhatrapati.
item.content:encoded:
Anshul Chhatrapati grew up knowing his father was different.

The name he inherited from him was itself a giveaway – Chhatrapati, a Sanskrit word for sovereign ruler, is most commonly associated with 17th century Maratha king, Chhatrapati Shivaji. That it was being used as a family name in Sirsa, a town in Haryana on the border with Punjab, was highly unusual.

“It was during his college days,” explained Anshul, speaking of his father Ram Chander Chhatrapati, “that one of his teachers had given him the title Chhatrapati for his leadership qualities and passion”.

It was Ram Chander Chhatrapati’s passion for truth and journalism that eventually cost him his life.

In October 2002, two assailants shot at him outside his home in Sirsa. As they fled, one was nabbed by the police. They turned out to be followers of Gurmeet Ram Rahim, a self-styled godman who had set up a religious organisation called the Dera Sacha Sauda, which had grown politically influential on the back of its following among the Dalits of Punjab and Haryana.

item.title: At BRICS summit, why Vladimir Putin went on diplomatic blitz with Global South leaders
item.description: The sanctions war between Russia and the West has made its economic and trade relations with the Global South pivotal for the country’s survival.
item.content:encoded:
Over the past two weeks, Russia’s President Vladimir Putin staged a major diplomatic blitz. Across three events in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Vladivostok in Russia’s Far East and New Delhi, India, as well as a state visit by Vietnam’s leader, he met with some 18 heads of state.

Among them were the leaders of heavyweights of the Global South such as China, India, Indonesia, Iran, Malaysia and Turkey, just to name a few.

The Ukraine war certainly featured in these conversations. Russia has recently ramped up its attacks on Ukraine, further fuelling some fears in the West that Ukraine could end up losing the war.

Tellingly, however, the main thrust of discussions led by the Russian president had a different focus: fuel, trade and transit.

Here’s why Russia is deepening ties with many partners in the Global South – and what these meetings tell us about the impacts of Western efforts to isolate Putin.

Fuel and energy security is becoming a mutual concern for both Moscow and its partners in the Global South. Ukraine’s deliberate offensive campaign targeting Russia’s oil refining capacity has resulted in noticeable fuel shortages in the country.

The Allahabad High Court on Wednesday ruled that a 31-year-old man who converted to Islam from Hinduism cannot be restrained by his birth family and upheld his freedom to choose his religion, Bar and Bench reported.

Justice Sandeep Jain noted that Ayush Malik had “voluntarily embraced Islam and that such decision was neither induced nor occasioned by any threat, coercion, undue influence or pressure”.

Jain said that there was “no lawful justification” for his continued restraint and allowed him to reside at a place of his choice.

item.title: Chhattisgarh: NIA court sentences 10 persons to death for 2013 Jhiram Valley Maoist attack
item.description: They have been convicted under the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act and sections of the Indian Penal Code pertaining to criminal conspiracy and murder.
item.content:encoded:
A National Investigation Agency court on Wednesday sentenced 10 persons to death for their role in the 2013 Jhiram Valley Maoist attack that killed 29 persons, including senior Congress leaders, The Indian Express reported.

They were convicted on September 5 under the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act and sections of the Indian Penal Code pertaining to criminal conspiracy and murder.

On May 25, 2013, more than 150 Maoists had ambushed a Congress convoy in Bastar’s Jhiram Ghati ahead of Assembly elections. Besides the deaths, around 28 persons had been injured.

Among those killed were the Congress’ state unit chief Nand Kumar Patel and his son Dinesh, and former MLA Uday Mudliyar.

Party leader Mahendra Karma, who played an instrumental role in organising the anti-Maoist state-sponsored militia Salwa Judum, was also killed in the attack.

The campaign was launched in 2005 to target villages seen as harbouring Maoists. Armed vigilantes allegedly torched homes and forced villagers to flee to government-run camps.

Translated as “purification hunt” in the Gondi language, Salwa Judum was presented by the state government as a spontaneous movement by the region’s Adivasi community against the Maoists.

However, human rights activists have accused the Salwa Judum of coercing residents into leaving their villages and supporting the group. With the tribal community split between both sides, there were several deaths over several months.
